composition: Nominal composition (wt%): Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–1.0Be, i.e. Fe balance, 30 Mn, 10 Al, 1.5 C and 1.0 Be. The base Fe–Mn–Al–C system relies on high Mn and C contents to stabilise austenite and preserve ductility while Al lowers density; Be is added as an additional lighter element (ρ = 1.848 g/cm³, atomic radius 111 pm) beyond the two conventional light additions (Al, ρ ≈ 2.7 g/cm³). In this alloy system Be is described as a ferritic-affinity element with a strong solid-solution-strengthening effect on ferrite, and along with Al it belongs to the elements that extend the ferrite phase region, so its addition shrinks the austenite field. All constituent elements were charged as high-purity metals: Fe, Mn, Al, C and Be each 99.99%.
conclusions: In this Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe study, 1.0 wt% Be is the composition at which the as-cast structure of the steel becomes a γ (FCC) + δ (BCC) duplex containing Be–Fe compound precipitates (Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe); the 0Be and 0.5Be counterparts remain fully austenitic, so the sample marks the onset of the Be-induced ferrite stabilisation that also raises the austenite microhardness monotonically across the series (475.80 ±13.75 HV here). Among the three constituents of the as-cast steel, the Be–Fe compound is the hardest (483.50 ±16.65 HV), ferrite the softest (437.40 ±15.72 HV), and the appearance of this softer ferrite is the reason the dual-phase alloys show a lower average matrix hardness despite each phase hardening with Be. In the wider context of the paper, adding 0.5–1.5 wt% Be lowered the density of the rolled steel to about 6.25–6.47 g/cm³ — some 19.87% below conventional steel grades (ρ ≈ 7.82 g/cm³) and 3.8% below unalloyed Fe–Mn–Al–C (ρ ≈ 6.50 g/cm³) — while strength, hardness and elongation were kept at a high level, a combination the authors state had not been achieved previously in the Fe–Mn–Al–C system; on an Ashby plot of strength–ductility product versus density the Be-bearing steels occupy the lowest-density, highest-product corner of the property space.
mechanisms: Be addition promotes ferrite formation: as Be content rises from 0/0.5 to 1.0/1.5 wt%, the as-cast XRD shows a markedly increased ferrite (110) reflection at 2θ ≈ 44.67° and the microstructure changes from single-phase austenite to γ + δ dual-phase, indicating Be stabilises the ferrite (BCC) phase in the Fe–Mn–Al–C matrix.

Solubility limit control of Be–Fe precipitation: Be has almost no solid solubility in austenite at room temperature and very limited solubility in ferrite (austenite can dissolve <1% Be, while ferrite can dissolve much more), so once the Be addition exceeds what the matrix can hold the excess Be is rejected and precipitates as Be–Fe compounds (Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe).

Local composition condition for compound formation: the Be–Fe phase is observed when the local mass percentage of Be to Fe reaches about 1:4; increasing the Be content raises the probability of Be–Fe atomic pairing and leads to segregation and formation of the Be–Fe phase, which explains why 1.0Be (but not 0Be/0.5Be) shows Be2Fe and Be12Fe peaks in addition to Be11Fe.

Site of Be–Fe precipitation: because Be is rejected from the saturated matrix, the Be–Fe compound nucleates preferentially at austenite/ferrite boundaries and in the remaining inter-island liquid, giving the observed widely distributed 'ancient Chinese character'-shaped precipitates at the γ/δ boundary in the as-cast 1.0Be structure.

Hardness of the as-cast matrix increases with Be content: part of the hardening is attributed to solid-solution strengthening by dissolved Be, and part to the formation of Be–Fe compounds; the effect is comparatively small in the fully austenitic alloys (0Be, 0.5Be) because a large increase in compound content produced only a modest hardness rise.

Dual-phase nature tempers the average matrix hardness: 0Be and 0.5Be are austenitic, whereas 1.0Be and 1.5Be are austenite + ferrite; since ferrite (437.40 HV) is softer than austenite (475.80 HV), the appearance of ferrite lowers the average matrix hardness even though each individual phase hardens with increasing Be.

Growth of the Be–Fe phase consumes austenite: in high-Be as-cast alloys the increasing amount of Be–Fe phase encroaches on the positions of the austenite matrix and occupies the original austenite sites, reducing the austenite content and, together with it, the ferrite content, which is why the ferrite in 1.5Be is finer than in 1.0Be.

Lattice-distortion origin of Be–Fe precipitation and of the limited density benefit: Be substitutes for Fe on the lattice but is undersized (111 pm vs 124 pm for Fe), so it distorts the lattice inward (shrinkage) while Al (143 pm) bows the lattice outward; inward distortion cannot expand the molar volume, so unlike Al, Be does not deliver a strong lightweighting effect, and once the accumulating distortion energy exceeds the solubility limit a new Be–Fe phase forms around the solid solution.

Lattice distortion also drives carbon out of solution: the inward lattice shrinkage caused by Be substitution changes the positions of some C atoms, expelling them from interstitial sites so that they can no longer remain in solid solution and instead precipitate as carbides on the matrix surface.
microstructure: As-cast 1.0Be is a three-constituent structure: austenite (γ, FCC) matrix + ferrite (δ, BCC) + Be–Fe compound precipitates. Optical microscopy shows a clearly dual-phase structure with large bright, blocky-to-vermiform δ islands embedded in the darker γ matrix, with dark inter-island regions identified as "beryllium compound"; ferrite is evenly distributed in the austenite matrix and the Be–Fe phase is randomly distributed. The Be–Fe precipitates occur as point-like, needle-like and rod-like particles and as "ancient Chinese character"-shaped precipitates that appear at the austenite/ferrite boundary and are widely distributed. XRD confirms the phase assemblage as austenite + ferrite + partial precipitates, with the ferrite (110) reflection at 2θ ≈ 44.67° clearly increased relative to the lower-Be alloys, evidencing that Be promotes ferrite formation; in 1.0Be the Be2Fe and Be12Fe peaks appear around the Be11Fe peaks, the identified Be–Fe compounds being Be11Fe, Be12Fe and Be2Fe. The defining microstructural evolution of the series is that the as-cast structure changes from single-phase austenite at 0Be and 0.5Be to a γ + δ dual-phase structure accompanied by Be–Fe compound precipitates at 1.0Be and 1.5Be. No grain size, volume fraction or texture values are reported for this as-cast state.
processing: Two-step route. (1) Melting/casting: high-purity Fe (99.99%), Mn (99.99%), Al (99.99%), C (99.99%) and Be (99.99%) were melted into alloy ingots in a vacuum induction melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere; the resulting ingot was 60 mm in diameter and 30 mm thick. (2) As-cast terminal state: the ingot was left as-cast, i.e. slow-cooled with no heat treatment and no thermal deformation applied. The paper notes that as-cast Fe–Mn–Al–C system steel without heat treatment and thermal deformation cannot obtain a uniform microstructure, so the as-cast condition here represents the unhomogenised solidification structure. For reference within the same study, the sibling strips of the series were subsequently hot rolled at 1050 °C to a 5 mm plate (about 83% total deformation in 17 passes, ~1.5 mm per pass, strain rate 0.6 s⁻¹, 3 min reheating between passes, water quenched after the final pass); that thermomechanical path is not part of this as-cast sample.
properties: Mechanical (as-cast, room temperature): Vickers microhardness measured with an FM-ARS9000 tester at 500 gf using a 15×5 matrix and the average of 25 points — austenite matrix 475.80 ±13.75 HV, ferrite 437.40 ±15.72 HV and Be–Fe phase 483.50 ±16.65 HV. Two features stand out: the Be–Fe compound is the hardest constituent, and ferrite is softer than the austenite matrix. The austenite hardness of the as-cast matrix increases with increasing Be content across the series (453.31 ±11.34 HV for 0Be, 462.88 ±13.84 HV for 0.5Be, 475.80 ±13.75 HV for 1.0Be, 479.74 ±11.99 HV for 1.5Be), the ferrite hardness in the two dual-phase alloys also rising with Be (437.40 → 452.54 HV from 1.0Be to 1.5Be). No tensile, density or other property values are reported for this as-cast sample. Characterization applied to the as-cast condition of the series: XRD (D/MAX-2500/PC, Cu Kα, 2θ = 20°–100°, 2°/min continuous scanning), optical microscopy (Axiovert 200 MAT, 8% nitrate-alcohol etch, 0.05 µm surface finish), SEM (Hitachi S-3400), TEM bright-field imaging with selected-area electron diffraction (JE-2100F, 200 kV; specimens thinned to 40 µm and dual-jet electropolished in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 26.5 V and −20 °C) and Vickers microhardness testing.
summary: As-cast 1.0Be is an Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C low-density steel ingot alloyed with 1.0 wt% beryllium, prepared by vacuum induction melting under high-purity argon and slow-cooled without any heat treatment or thermal deformation. It belongs to a study that introduced Be (ρ = 1.848 g/cm³), a ferrite-stabilising and lightweight element, into the Fe–Mn–Al–C system in order to push the density below the ~6.40 g/cm³ ceiling reached by Al and C alloying alone. The 1.0 wt% Be composition is the level at which the as-cast structure of this steel becomes dual-phase austenite (γ) + ferrite (δ) with Be–Fe compound precipitates, so the central question for this sample is how Be partitions between the austenite matrix, the newly formed ferrite and the Be–Fe compound, and how that partition changes the local hardness of each phase.
unmapped: A density of 6.36 ±0.04 g/cm³ is the value listed for 1.0Be, but it appears in Table 3, which is captioned 'Tensile experiment of rolling (1050 °C) Fe–30Mn–10Al–1.5C–xBe steels'; its attribution to the as-cast rather than the rolled state is therefore ambiguous and it has not been assigned to this sample's property section.

The DSC phase-transformation peak of the 1.0Be alloy is 1163.3 °C, approximately 1 °C lower than that of 0.5Be (1165.9 °C); however this DSC was recorded on heating after homogenisation, not on the as-cast state, and the text quotes 1278.8 °C for the Be-free steel whereas the printed DSC label reads 1320 °C.

A calculated equilibrium Fe–Be binary phase diagram (Fig. 19) showing stoichiometric line compounds FeBe12 (~0.13), FeBe5 (~0.17) and FeBe2 (~0.33) with invariant lines near 1150, 1050 and 680 °C is used as a thermodynamic rationale for Be partitioning; it is a general calculation for the Fe–Be system, not sample-specific data.

Rolled-state properties of the same alloy (for contrast, not part of this as-cast sample): 1050 °C hot-rolled 1.0Be gives YS 820.57 MPa, UST 1074.33 MPa, total elongation 30.71%, austenite hardness 398.39 ±14.630 HV and ferrite hardness 349.81 ±21.267 HV, with a grain size centred near 10 µm and a banded α + γ structure containing κ-carbide replaced by Be2C precipitates.

TEM/SAED identification of the as-cast precipitates (Be12Fe, 5–10 µm, along [−113] and [001]; and mutually perpendicular coarse Be12Fe with an AlFe3 [011] pattern) is reported for the as-cast 0.5Be and 1.5Be alloys in the paper; no TEM micrograph or diffraction pattern is presented specifically for the as-cast 1.0Be alloy.

The identity of 'beryllium compound' labels in OM and the exact stoichiometry of the Be–Fe phase in this particular sample are inferred from XRD peak positions (Be11Fe, Be12Fe, Be2Fe) rather than from a direct composition measurement of the individual precipitates.
